title: She Won the Right to Brancusi's Archive. Then She Wouldn't Let Anyone See It.
standfirst: Natalia Dumitresco spent decades as one of two people Constantin Brancusi trusted with everything he owned, and just as long refusing the French state access to it — a fight she won in court and kept fighting anyway, right up to the retrospective built to honour him.

sections.heading: A Retrospective Held Hostage in Its Final Year
sections.body: In the spring of 1994, curators preparing the largest Brancusi retrospective ever staged found they could not do their jobs. The show was booked into the Centre Pompidou for April 1995 and due to travel to Philadelphia afterward, and its scientific catalogue needed access to the sculptor's letters, drafts and photographs. Nobody could get to them. The papers were controlled by Natalia Dumitresco, by then the sole survivor of the couple Constantin Brancusi had named his universal heirs, and she was not handing them over. A reporter from [Le Journal des Arts](https://www.lejournaldesarts.fr/actualites/limbroglio-brancusi-104082) reached her anyway. She dismissed the Pompidou's own staff as "des gens bizarres" — odd people — she did not understand, and said they should be thanking her, not investigating her, for having conserved the archive at all ("me remercier d'avoir conservé ces archives"). The documents, she added, were with a notary and would surface in a forthcoming book. She would not say which publisher.

sections.heading: A Will Signed Eleven Months Before He Died
sections.body: On 12 April 1956, inside his studio at 11 Impasse Ronsin, Brancusi signed a will legalised by the notary Claude Burthe-Mique. Read literally, it left the French state almost nothing but stone and bronze — in the document's own words, "à l'État français, pour le Musée national d'art moderne... absolument tout ce que contiendront au jour de son décès ses ateliers, n'exceptant que l'argent comptant, les titres ou valeurs qui pourraient s'y trouver et qui reviendront à ses légataires universels": to the French state, for the National Museum of Modern Art, everything his studios held on the day of his death, except the cash, securities and valuables, which would go to his universal heirs. Those heirs were named in the same clause: the artist Alexandre Istrati and his wife, Natalia Dumitresco, who lived next door and had spent Brancusi's last years looking after him. The state's inheritance came with a condition attached — it had to rebuild the studio exactly as he left it, ideally inside the museum itself, and a doctor, Pascu Atanasiu, was named executor to see that through. Brancusi died eleven months later, on 16 March 1957. His heirs moved fast. By 3 October 1957 — under seven months on — Istrati and Dumitresco were already attaching two conditions of their own before releasing anything at all: that the atelier reconstruction be finished, and that the state recognise their own right to reproduce the works it had just inherited. That same year, the director of the Musées de France, Georges Salles, refused Istrati permission to take plaster casts and moulds out of the studio to make prints.

sections.heading: They Sued the State Over a Dead Man's Copies — and Won
sections.body: Salles's refusal set the pattern for the next four decades. The Réunion des musées nationaux held that Brancusi had never wanted his sculptures editioned at all — that unlike the reproducible bronzes of Rodin or Giacometti, a Brancusi casting was meant to stay a single, unrepeatable object. Margit Rowell, who later co-curated the 1995 retrospective, put the museums' position to Le Journal des Arts this way: "de nombreux témoignages prouvent que Brancusi ne souhaitait pas d'édition de son œuvre, qu'une fonte devait rester pour lui une pièce unique" — many accounts show Brancusi did not want his work editioned; for him, a casting had to remain unique. On that reading, the museums refused to authorise casting or moulding of anything Brancusi had left them, and reportedly opposed even a plan to install a cast of his Grand Coq beneath I. M. Pei's new glass pyramid at the Louvre. None of it held up in court. Istrati and Dumitresco sued for their reproduction rights; the Réunion des musées nationaux, backed by the estate's own executor, fought back. The museums won at first instance. They lost on appeal. They lost again when France's Cour de cassation threw out their final challenge. From that point on, the right to license a Brancusi reproduction belonged in law to the heirs, not the state holding the sculptures. It was that same right, and nothing else, that let one widow decide, in 1994, whether a museum's own curators got to see a dead man's letters.

sections.heading: Two Painters Who Won the Same Prize Two Years Apart
sections.body: Natalia Dumitresco was born in Bucharest in December 1915 and trained at the city's Academy of Fine Arts. She married Alexandre Istrati in 1939, and the couple reached Paris in 1947 — it was there, not in Romania, that both found their footing as painters, showing with the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles, the showcase built for postwar abstraction that took its bearings from Kandinsky and Alberto Magnelli. Istrati won the Kandinsky Prize in 1953. Two years later, in 1955, his wife won it too. She followed that with the Carnegie Prize in Pittsburgh in 1959, and by the end of the decade was showing in Brussels and Cologne as well as Paris. None of this depended on Brancusi, who by 1955 had less than two years left to live and who, so far as the record shows, never publicly promoted either of their painting careers. Whatever he left this couple, it was not reputation — the reputation, such as it became, they built showing alongside each other in the same Paris salons that were making room for abstraction after the war.

sections.heading: A Grid Filed Under a Word That Means Formless
sections.body: This corpus lists Tout à la joie under Colour Field painting. WikiArt's own page for the picture calls it Art Informel instead. Neither sits comfortably with what a specialist account of Dumitresco's actual working method describes. The women's-art archive AWARE characterises her mature style as "austere and rigorous," built from "modulations of geometric frameworks – squares, grids, stripes, meshes, circles, rectangles, diamonds," with "armatures and quadrangular cells" that structure the canvas into something closer to a maze than a mood. That is close to the opposite of what Art Informel means: the term describes the postwar European painters — Wols, Fautrier, the early Tàpies — who abandoned composition and geometry altogether in favour of gesture and raw material. A grid is not formless; a grid is one of the more formal things a painter can put on a canvas. Colour Field fits a little better on one count — Dumitresco did, by this account, spend years working in black and white before she "tackled the problem of colours," and Tout à la joie, painted in 1970 under a title that promises something close to pure joy, belongs to that later, brighter decade. But Colour Field's American exponents built paintings from a handful of unbroken fields of hue, not the meshes and cells AWARE describes. The plainer answer may be that Dumitresco painted in a manner specific enough that neither label quite holds her.

sections.heading: The Fight Outlived Both of Them
sections.body: Istrati died in 1991. Dumitresco died in Chars, north-west of Paris, in July 1997, at eighty-one — three years after telling a reporter to thank her for guarding Brancusi's papers, and having never, so far as the record shows, handed over the archive she had said would surface in a book. The collection and its copyright passed to their nephew, Theodor Nicol, who now manages reproduction rights through the French collecting society ADAGP. The dispute did not end with her. In 2021 the Romanian politician [Iulian Popescu began preparing a lawsuit](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2021/05/19/romanian-politician-gears-up-to-sue-brancusis-heir-over-longstanding-copyright-battle) against Nicol on behalf of Târgu Jiu, the town that owns three Brancusi monuments outright — including the Endless Column — but cannot legally sell a postcard of them without Nicol's permission. Popescu's argument turns on the same question that has trailed this estate since 1957: Romanian copyright law in force when Brancusi died protected an heir's rights for fifteen years, which by his reading put the works into the public domain around 1972, decades before the 1996 law Nicol's side now relies on. Whether that argument succeeds is, as far as any source confirms, still unresolved. What is certain is where the fight's first winners ended up: Istrati and Dumitresco are buried with Brancusi, in the same grave, at the Cimetière du Montparnasse — the closest thing this fifty-year argument has to a resting point.
